newsitem.title: USA: Gillette sees $80-$120 mln in deal synergies.
newsitem.headline: Gillette sees $80-$120 mln in deal synergies.

text.p: Gillette Co chairman and chief executive Alfred Zeien said the $7 billion planned acquisition of Duracell International Inc is expected to yield $80 to $120 million in savings in two years.

The cost of the merger, the result of talks that began in January, are expected to be $275 million, which is "not a hard number" subject to adjustment, and excludes another $55 million in one-time closing costs.
Zeien also said Warren Buffett, whose Berkshire Hathaway owns 11 percent of Gillette backs the merger, which remains subject to approval by both companies' shareholders.

The transaction will accelerate Gillette's rate of per share earnings growth -- almost 18 percent last year -- and will be accretive to earnings to per share "from day one, even without the syneries," Zeien said in a conference call with reporters and analysts.
He declined to provide specific projections on the earnings growth rate and accretion.
Kohlberg Kravis & Roberts Co's 34 percent stake in Duracell will be translated into a 6.8 percent stake in the post-merger Gillette, Zeien said.
Also, KKR's Henry Kravis has been extended an invitation to join Gillette's board, an offer that Kravis not yet decided on, the chairman said.
Meanwhile, investors bought into the combination.
Gillette slumped as low at 63, a two point loss, preceding the formal announcement of the deal, then turned around to hit a new year-high 66-7/8 in midday trade after it was unvieled.
Terms of the deal call for a stock swap at a ratio of 0.904 Gillette share for every Duracell shares, and Zeien said he expects the deal to close by mid-December, assuming shareholder approval.
Based on Wednesday's closing prices, the terms value Duracell at about $58.76 per share.
On the New York Stock Exchange, Duracell shares were the most active issue, up 9-5/8 to 58, easing off an earlier all-time high 59-1/8.
Gillette was the NYSE's second most-active stock.
Zeien said Gillette established a set of criteria five years ago to find an acquisition that would add "another leg" to its global consumer products business.
A review was completed last fall and Duracell "met and exceeded the criteria.

The criteria include Duracell's worldwide leadership position in the alkaline battery business, its technology orientation, the "essentially recession-resistant" nature of the business and the "inter-changability of managements," he said.
In December, 1995, he said he presented the idea to the Gillette board, and was then authorized to approach Duracell with the idea.

"I said (to Duracell) it would have to be a pooling of interest (transaction), so we had to find an exchange ratio between our shares and Duracell shares that was beneficial to both groups. We found that combination recently, and then things moved very quickly," he said.
